stops.name: Buenos Aires, elected to the Argentine Academy of Letters
stops.campa: The Academia Argentina de Letras, founded in 1931 the same year as Sur and closed to women through the whole of its first forty-five years, elects Victoria as its first female member. The honor arrives late, in her eighty-sixth year, and under a military dictatorship she will have as little patience for as she had for Perón's government two decades before; she accepts it nonetheless as a recognition owed not to her alone but to the two generations of Argentine women writers, her sister Silvina among them, whom the Academy's closed doors had refused to see.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, formally seated at the Academy
stops.campa: Victoria takes her seat at the Academia Argentina de Letras in a formal induction ceremony, the first woman in the institution's forty-six-year history to do so. She delivers her discourse as she has delivered every public act of her long life, in the register of exactness rather than false modesty, naming the work of Sur and Editorial Sur as the credential that qualifies her, more than any single book of her own, for the chair. Twice nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1970 and 1974, she has never won it; this seat is the nearest thing her own country offers to that recognition.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, writing the incomplete Autobiografía
stops.campa: In the same years that bracket her imprisonment, Victoria works at an autobiography she will never finish to her own satisfaction, six volumes eventually assembled and published only after her death, beginning with El archipiélago, the childhood recalled in the register of scattered islands rather than a single continuous land. She writes of her sisters, her governesses, the forbidden stage, the marriage, Julián Martínez, Tagore, with the same unsparing exactness she has always demanded of the writers Sur published; it is the last major work of her life, and the most private.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death at eighty-eight
stops.campa: Victoria dies in Buenos Aires at eighty-eight, having outlived Tagore by more than four decades, Woolf by thirty-eight years, Ortega by twenty-four, Camus by nineteen, Drieu by thirty-four; having outlasted a marriage, an eighteen-year clandestine love, two governments that imprisoned or surveilled her, and every rival literary review Buenos Aires produced against Sur across four decades. She is the last of the great bridge-builders of her generation between the Río de la Plata and the wider republic of letters, and very nearly the only one who built the bridge with her own inherited fortune rather than a government's or a university's.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Recoleta, laid among the founders
stops.campa: Victoria is buried in the Cementerio de la Recoleta, the necropolis of the Buenos Aires families whose names built the republic she was born into and, in her own fashion, spent her whole life quietly arguing with and enlarging. Sur itself will run another thirteen years without her before closing in 1992 at 372 numbers; Villa Ocampo stands open to the public in Beccar; the correspondences with Tagore, Woolf, Ortega, Camus, Keyserling, and Drieu la Rochelle are gathered, volume by volume, into the record of a life spent making sure that no single country's letters had to be read alone.
